newsitem.title: USA: U.S. chides Europe for opposing its anti-Cuba law.
newsitem.headline: U.S. chides Europe for opposing its anti-Cuba law.

text.p: The United States said on Monday it was not appropriate for Europe to retaliate against a controversial law tightening the U.S. economic embargo on Cuba by discouraging investment by other countries.

"We believe Helms-Burton can be implemented in a way that satisfies international obligations, those of the U.S. We don't believe it's appropriate for the Europeans to retaliate," State Department spokesman Nicholas Burns told reporters.
Burns was responding to a decision by European Union foreign ministers earlier on Monday to make it illegal for Europeans to obey Washington's anti-Cuba Helms-Burton Act.
Burns faulted the Europeans for not joining the United States in pressing harder for democracy and improved human rights on the communist-ruled Caribbean island.

"We wish the Europeans also had an expressed public interest and made a priority the situation of the many many people in Cuba whose rights are being denied by the Castro government ... We'd like to see more talk from the Europeans about democracy in Cuba," he said.
The Helms-Burton Act, passed earlier this year, angered some of Washington's closest allies and main trade partners.

But it helped solidify President Bill Clinton's political support among Cuban-Americans, many of whom live in Florida, a crucial state in the Nov. 5 presidential election. The state normally votes Republican, but Clinton is hoping to win this time and is running a close race.

The Helms-Burton law allows lawsuits to be filed in U.S. courts against foreign firms that own or operate properties seized by Cuba from U.S. citizens who were Cuban nationals before the 1959 communist revolution.
Last July Clinton ordered the sanctions to come into force but delayed implementation for six months to appease U.S. allies who threatened retaliation.

The law also allows denial of visas to shareholders and officers of foreign firms operating these properties in Cuba and this provision has already been used to punish a Canadian mining company and a Mexican telecommunications firm.
The European Union's law will prohibit European individuals or companies from complying with the U.S. measure and allow them to reclaim damages in EU courts.

Clinton last summer appointed Undersecretary of Commerce Stuart Eizenstat to try to placate the allies and persuade them to make common cause in pressuring Cuban leader Fidel Castro to make democratic, human rights and economic reforms.
U.S. officials have hinted that if Europe, Mexico and Canada cooperate in this regard, Clinton may waive the lawsuits provision in February.
The United States acknowledged last week, however, that Eizenstat's efforts have so far failed. Nevertheless he is now on another mission to Europe.
